metadata.title: Pinhole: high-level design for photo sharing

nodes.title: High-level design only: Pinhole photo sharing

content.markdown:
Pinhole lets people post photos and see photos from the accounts they follow, sized for about 2 million daily active users at launch.

This canvas shows parts, responsibilities, connections and reasons. Code, internal modules and operations are left to each service's low-level design.

content.label: Clients
content.takeaway: Two thin apps on one public HTTPS API

content.label: Mobile app
details: Public HTTPS API; simple input checks only
Uploads originals with a short-lived signed URL

content.label: Web app
details: Public HTTPS API; simple input checks only

content.label: Edge & API
content.takeaway: One way in: TLS, token check, rate limit, routing

content.label: API gateway
content.sublabel: Single way in for client requests
details: Rate limit: 120 requests per minute per account
Fails closed: rejects the request when auth can't be reached
Routes to the right service; never serves photo bytes

content.label: Core services
content.takeaway: Auth, upload and feed own the synchronous work

content.label: Upload service
content.sublabel: Signs upload URLs and records new photos
details: Records a new photo as 'processing' once the upload completes

content.label: Feed service
content.sublabel: Builds each person's feed from the accounts they follow
details: On PhotoReady: adds the photo to followers' feeds and requests follower alerts

content.label: Asynchronous processing
content.takeaway: Upload and processing only meet through the queue

content.label: Message queue
details: Keeps events up to 7 days: a processing outage delays thumbnails but loses no uploads

content.label: Media processing workers
details: Read the original, write the thumbnails back
Mark the photo 'ready', then publish PhotoReady
A photo that keeps failing stays 'processing' and is never shown in a feed

content.label: Storage
content.takeaway: The metadata database is the source of truth; the cache is a copy

content.label: Metadata database
content.sublabel: Source of truth: follow relationships, photo records and processing status

content.label: Cache
details: Only a copy kept for speed: losing it makes feeds slower, never wrong

content.label: External (outside the Pinhole boundary)
content.takeaway: Run by third parties; Pinhole only sends them requests

content.label: CDN
content.sublabel: Third party: serves photos and thumbnails close to the user

content.label: Push-notification provider
content.sublabel: Third party: delivers alerts; Pinhole doesn't control when they arrive

content.label: Design decisions
content.takeaway: Why the system has this shape

nodes.title: A queue keeps thumbnails from failing uploads

content.markdown:
A slow or failed thumbnail job must never block or fail an upload, so the upload service and the workers only meet through the message queue.

**Cost:** a new photo takes a few seconds to appear in feeds.

nodes.title: Signed URLs keep big files off the gateway

content.markdown: Originals can be up to 25 MB; routing them through the gateway would make it the bottleneck. Clients send bytes straight to object storage; the upload service only signs the URL and records the result.

nodes.title: Metadata lives apart from photo bytes

content.markdown: Bytes go to object storage, everything queried goes to the metadata database: the two grow at very different rates and need different backups.
Feed pages are cached for speed only; the metadata database stays the source of truth, so the cache can be flushed at any time.

nodes.title: Buy CDN and push delivery, don't build them

content.markdown: A third-party CDN and push-notification provider instead of our own; their outages are accepted as outside our control.
How failed processing is retried, and when a stuck photo is cleaned up, is not decided yet.

nodes.title: Open: precomputed feeds for big accounts

content.markdown: Whether the feed service should precompute feeds for accounts with very many followers is left to the feed service's own low-level design.
